title: Physical vs Chemical Changes
description: How to distinguish between changes that make new substances and those that do not.

notes.heading: Physical Changes
notes.body: A physical change alters the form or appearance of a substance without changing what it is made of — no new substances are produced. Usually reversible. Examples: melting ice (still H₂O), dissolving sugar in water, cutting paper. Changes of state (solid ↔ liquid ↔ gas) are always physical changes.

notes.heading: Chemical Changes
notes.body: A chemical change produces one or more new substances with different chemical properties. Usually difficult or impossible to reverse. Signs: colour change, gas produced (bubbling), temperature change, light produced, new smell. Examples: burning wood, rusting iron, cooking an egg, photosynthesis, neutralisation.

notes.heading: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
notes.body: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings — the temperature rises. Examples: burning fuels, respiration, neutralisation. Endothermic reactions absorb heat — temperature drops. Examples: thermal decomposition, dissolving ammonium nitrate. In energy profile diagrams, exothermic reactions have products at lower energy than reactants; endothermic have products at higher energy.

flashcards.definition: A change that alters the form of a substance but does not produce any new substances. Usually reversible.
A change that produces one or more new substances with different properties. Usually irreversible.
A chemical reaction that releases energy (as heat) to the surroundings, causing the temperature to rise.
A chemical reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, causing the temperature to fall.
flashcards.example: Dissolving ammonium nitrate (used in cold packs).

flashcards.definition: The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products in a chemical reaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a PHYSICAL change?
questions.explanation: Melting ice is a physical change — still H₂O, just a different state.

questions.stem: Which observation is the BEST evidence that a chemical change has occurred?
choices: The shape of the material changes
A new gas is produced and a colour change occurs
questions.explanation: Producing a new gas and a colour change both suggest new substances have formed.

questions.stem: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to the temperature of the surroundings?
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat → surroundings get hotter.

questions.stem: A student mixes two solutions and notices the temperature drops. What type of reaction is this?
questions.explanation: If temperature drops, the reaction is absorbing heat — endothermic.

questions.stem: According to conservation of mass, if 10 g of calcium carbonate reacts and 4.4 g of CO₂ escapes, what is the total mass of remaining products?
questions.explanation: 10 – 4.4 = 5.6 g. Mass is conserved — it doesn't disappear with the gas.
